_note: Prerendered library and the single source of truth for explanation text. The bridge sends an id plus summary/steps/lenses built from this file; the glasses app reads it directly. A chapter is one lens. 'knobs' has one entry per step: what up/down changes on that step (axis x or y of the scene, or null). 'spec' is the drawing data for data-driven scenes (flow, number). 'unknown' = not in the library.

objects.label: Guitar string
objects.detect_hint: a guitar, ukulele or any plucked string instrument, or a close-up of strings and frets
objects.concept: Standing waves: a shorter string vibrates faster, so the note is higher
objects.answer: A shorter string vibrates faster, so the note is higher.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Up/down: turn it.
captions: Pluck one string and the whole guitar sings. The sound starts in the string.
A guitar is six strings over a hollow wooden box with a thin top.
A plucked string swings back and forth hundreds of times a second, but moves little air.
The string shakes the bridge, the bridge shakes the wide top, and the top pushes air.
Pressing a fret shortens the string, so it swings faster and the note rises.
110 swings every second: the open A string. Fret 12 halves it to 220.

chapters.title: Standing waves
chapters.hint: Up/down: change it. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Pressing a fret shortens the string. Half the length gives double the frequency, so the note is one octave higher.
A string also vibrates in whole-number patterns: harmonics n = 1, 2, 3 at f, 2f, 3f.
Wave speed depends on tension T and mass per length: f = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu). Tighter = higher.

chapters.title: What if
chapters.lead: Every fret raises the note by the same ratio.
chapters.hint: Up/down: fret. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Each fret shortens the string and raises the note by about 6 percent. Twelve frets double the frequency: one octave.
A string twice as long sounds one octave lower at every fret. That is partly why bass instruments are big.

chapters.title: Follow the sound
chapters.lead: A tiny string cannot move much air. The wooden body can.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: A pluck pulls the string aside and lets go. The string swings back and forth at its own frequency.
The string is too thin to push much air by itself. It shakes the bridge it is tied to instead.
The bridge shakes the thin soundboard. Its large area moves a lot of air, which makes the note loud.
Pressure waves travel through the air at 343 metres per second to your ear.

losses.label: Most becomes heat, a little is sound

chapters.title: The number
chapters.lead: An open A string swings 110 times every second.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Frequency counts swings per second. The open A string of a guitar makes 110 of them: 110 hertz.
Fret 12 halves the string, so the note doubles to 220 Hz. The wave runs along the string at 143 m/s.
Each doubling is one octave. Two octaves above this string is the 440 Hz that orchestras tune to.

headline.label: an open A string, swings per second

rows.label: Length of the sound wave in air

compare.label: Concert pitch A, two octaves up

objects.label: Thrown ball
objects.detect_hint: any ball (tennis, football, basketball, bouncy ball, crumpled paper ball) held, thrown or bouncing
objects.concept: Projectile motion and bounce: gravity bends the path into a parabola; each bounce keeps only part of the energy
objects.answer: Gravity bends the path into a curve.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Up/down: turn it.
captions: Every thrown ball curves back to the ground. Two forces shape the whole flight.
Inside the cover: a rubber bladder of air pumped above the outside pressure.
Gravity pulls down all the time, so the upward speed shrinks, stops, then reverses.
Air pushes against the motion and steals speed, so the real throw lands shorter.
On a bounce the squeezed air works like a spring and throws the ball back up.
Thrown at 10 metres per second and 45 degrees, it lands about 10 metres away.

number.label: range of a 10 m/s throw, no air

chapters.title: Projectile motion
chapters.hint: Up/down: change it. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Gravity pulls the ball down all the time, so its path curves into a parabola.
Without air, sideways speed never changes. Only the up-and-down speed does, because gravity acts down.
Air drag slows the ball, so the best angle drops below 45 degrees. The faint path shows the same throw without air.

chapters.title: Bounce
chapters.lead: Each bounce keeps only part of the energy.
chapters.hint: Up/down: change it. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Each bounce is lower than the last, because the ball keeps only part of its energy every time it hits the floor.
Falling turns height energy into movement; the squash stores it like a spring; some is lost as heat and sound every bounce.
Bounciness depends on the material: a super ball springs back almost fully, clay absorbs the energy as heat and barely bounces.

chapters.title: What if
chapters.lead: Change the angle, then change the planet.
chapters.hint: Up/down: angle. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Change the angle. A flat throw and a steep throw both fall short. Without air, 45 degrees goes farthest.
On the Moon gravity is six times weaker, so every throw flies six times as far. The best angle is still 45.

chapters.title: Follow the energy
chapters.lead: The energy changes form but never disappears.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Your arm does work on the ball. A tennis ball thrown at 10 metres per second carries about 2.9 joules.
Going up, motion energy turns into height energy. At the top of a 45 degree throw it is half and half.
Coming down, height energy turns back into motion. Air drag takes some, about a tenth for a tennis ball.
On landing the motion energy becomes heat, sound and the next bounce. None of it is destroyed.

chapters.title: The number
chapters.lead: A 10 m/s throw at 45 degrees lands about 10 metres away.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Thrown at 10 metres per second and 45 degrees, a ball lands about 10 metres away, if air is ignored.
It stays up for 1.4 seconds and peaks at 2.5 metres. Range is speed squared divided by g: 100 over 9.81.
The Moon pulls six times more weakly, so the same throw flies six times as far: about 62 metres.

headline.label: how far a 10 m/s throw at 45 degrees flies

compare.label: The same throw on the Moon flies

objects.label: Bike gears
objects.detect_hint: a bicycle, its chain, chainring, cassette or rear gears
objects.concept: Gear ratio: a big front and small back gear trades pedalling force for speed
objects.answer: A big front gear and small back gear trade force for speed.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Up/down: turn it.
captions: One turn of the pedals can carry a bike over six metres. Gears decide how far.
Pedals turn a big front chainring; the chain carries its turning to a small rear cog.
48 teeth in front, 16 behind: the rear wheel turns three times per pedal turn.
The price: the wheel turns faster, but the tyre pushes the road far more gently.
Each wheel turn rolls about 2.1 metres, so one pedal turn moves you 6.3 metres.
At 80 pedal turns a minute, that is 30 kilometres an hour.

chapters.title: Gear ratio
chapters.hint: Up/down: change it. Left/right: next lens.
captions: The chain links a big front gear to a small rear gear, so one pedal turn spins the wheel more than once.
Gear ratio is front teeth divided by rear teeth. Each pedal turn pulls that many teeth of chain past the rear gear.
Energy is conserved: a higher ratio gives more speed per pedal turn but less push at the wheel.

chapters.title: What if
chapters.lead: Fewer teeth at the back, more speed per pedal turn.
chapters.hint: Up/down: rear teeth. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Fewer teeth at the back give more speed for the same pedalling: 44 km/h on the smallest gear, 14 on the largest.
The small front ring lowers every gear by about 30 percent. You go slower, but each push on the pedal is stronger.

chapters.title: Follow the force
chapters.lead: Your push travels through the chain to the road.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Your leg pushes the pedal down. The crank is a lever that turns the push into a twist on the front gear.
The front gear pulls the top of the chain tight. A clean chain loses only about 3 percent to friction.
The chain turns the rear gear. A small rear gear spins the wheel several times for every pedal turn.
The tyre pushes back on the road and the road pushes the bike forward. That push is what moves you.

chapters.title: The number
chapters.lead: One pedal turn in a high gear carries you over 6 metres.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: The front gear has three times the teeth of the rear, so the wheel turns three times per pedal turn: 6.3 metres.
At 80 pedal turns a minute that is 30 km/h. The price: the tyre pushes with only 17 percent of your pedal force.
A low gear swaps it round. Three times the push for climbing, but only 2.1 metres per turn.

headline.label: forward per pedal turn, 48 teeth front, 16 rear

objects.label: Boiling kettle
objects.detect_hint: a kettle, pot of water, or a cup or mug of hot drink
objects.concept: Convection: hot water rises, cool water sinks, bubbles are water turning to vapour
objects.answer: Hot water rises, cool water sinks, bubbles are vapour.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.hint: Pinch: next. Up: replay. Down: back.
captions: A kettle brings a litre of water to the boil in about three minutes.
Inside: a heating element under the floor, the water, and a steam switch.
Current forced through the element's resistance turns electrical energy into heat.
Water touching the hot floor expands, gets lighter and rises; cooler water sinks.
Steam reaches a bimetal disc that bends when hot and snaps the power off.
2000 joules every second: enough to warm a litre by half a degree.

chapters.title: Convection and boiling
chapters.hint: Up/down: change it. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Heated water expands and gets lighter, so it rises in the middle and sinks at the sides.
Hot spots at the bottom let vapour bubbles form (nucleation), then they rise and burst.
At 100 °C extra energy goes into turning water to vapour, not heating it. That is latent heat.

chapters.title: Cut open
chapters.lead: An element, moving water, and a switch that feels the steam.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Under the floor of the jug sits the heating element: a coil of wire that gets hot when current flows.
Water touching the hot floor warms, rises up the middle, cools at the top and sinks at the sides.
When it boils, steam runs down a tube to a metal strip in the base. The strip bends and clicks the power off.

chapters.title: What if
chapters.lead: Twice the water takes about twice the time.
chapters.hint: Up/down: litres. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Boiling time grows almost in a straight line with the water. Twice the water needs about twice the time and energy.
Water that starts at 60 °C needs only half the heating, so it boils in half the time.

chapters.title: Follow the energy
chapters.lead: Electricity in, hot water and a little wasted heat out.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Electricity flows from the socket into a coil of wire in the base: the heating element.
The element resists the current, so all of the electrical energy turns into heat, which passes into the water.
About 88 percent ends up in the water. The rest warms the jug and the air around it.
At 100 °C the water turns to steam. The steam heats a metal strip that bends and clicks the kettle off.

chapters.title: The number
chapters.lead: Boiling a litre takes about a tenth of a kilowatt-hour.
chapters.hint: Up/down: litres. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Heating one litre of water by 80 degrees takes 335 kilojoules. From the socket that is about 0.11 kWh.
A 2 kW kettle needs about three minutes for it, and it costs about two cents.
The same energy would light a 10 watt LED lamp for more than ten hours. Boil only what you need.

headline.label: to boil this much water from 20 °C

compare.label: Same energy runs a 10 W LED lamp for

objects.label: Swinging keys
objects.detect_hint: keys on a lanyard or string, a necklace, a yo-yo, anything hanging that can swing
objects.concept: Pendulum: the swing time depends on the length, not the weight
objects.answer: Swing time depends on length, not weight.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Up/down: turn it.
captions: Keys swinging on a lanyard keep a steady beat, wide swings or small.
Just three things matter here: the pivot, the length of the lanyard, and gravity.
Gravity pulls the keys back toward the middle, so they speed up as they fall.
At the bottom they are fastest, overshoot, climb the other side and slow to a stop.
Heavier keys swing in the same time; only the length changes the beat.
25 cm of lanyard: one swing there and back takes about one second.

chapters.title: Swing time
chapters.hint: Up/down: change it. Left/right: next lens.
captions: For small swings, the time of one swing depends only on the length. A longer string swings more slowly.
The angle follows a smooth sine wave with T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g). Four times the length gives double the period.
Mass cancels out: two bobs of different mass on equal strings swing together.

chapters.title: What if
chapters.lead: A longer string swings more slowly, but not in proportion.
chapters.hint: Up/down: length. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Make the string longer and the swing slows, but the curve flattens. Four times the length only doubles the time.
On the Moon the same string swings about two and a half times more slowly, because gravity pulls back more gently.

chapters.title: Follow the energy
chapters.lead: Height energy and motion energy swap back and forth.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Lifting the keys to one side stores height energy. Nothing moves yet.
Let go: height energy turns into motion. At the bottom it is all motion: half a metre per second for a 20 degree swing.
On the far side the keys climb again and motion turns back into height. Then it all runs in reverse.
Each swing the air takes a little energy away as heat, so the swings shrink. The swing time stays the same.

losses.label: Air drag, a little each swing

chapters.title: The number
chapters.lead: Keys on a 25 cm lanyard swing back and forth every second.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Keys on a 25 centimetre lanyard swing there and back in about one second.
Swing time is 2 pi times the square root of length over g. Four times the length doubles it. Weight changes nothing.
Weaker gravity pulls back more gently. On the Moon the same lanyard needs two and a half seconds.

headline.label: one full swing, there and back, on a 25 cm string

rows.label: Speed at the bottom, 20 degree swing

compare.label: The same keys on the Moon swing in

objects.label: Smartphone
objects.detect_hint: a smartphone or tablet, front or back, in a hand or on a table
objects.concept: Layers: glass, touch sensor, OLED pixels, battery and logic board stacked in a few millimetres
objects.answer: About nine thin layers: glass, touch, pixels, chips and a battery.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Up/down: turn it.
captions: A phone packs a computer, a radio and a battery into under a centimetre.
Under the glass: a touch grid, a light-making display, a circuit board and a battery.
Your finger changes the electric field at the grid's crossing wires, so the phone knows where.
Each OLED pixel makes its own light; a black pixel is simply switched off.
Lithium ions move inside the battery and push current through the chips.
15 watt-hours in a full battery: a 2 kW kettle uses that in 28 seconds.

chapters.title: Layers
chapters.hint: Up/down: change it. Left/right: next lens.
captions: A phone is a sandwich of about nine thin layers, all packed into less than a centimetre.
The touch sensor is a grid of electrodes. Your finger changes the electric field, or capacitance, where you touch.
Millions of OLED pixels each make their own light. A black pixel is simply off, which saves power on dark screens.
The logic board holds processor, memory and radio chips. The processor does billions of simple steps per second.
Lithium ions move between two electrode layers as you charge and use the phone. The battery is the largest part inside.
The coil charges without a cable by magnetic induction. The camera stacks several lenses onto a tiny sensor.

chapters.title: What if
chapters.lead: A stronger charger fills the battery sooner.
chapters.hint: Up/down: charger. Left/right: next lens.
captions: A 5 watt charger needs over three hours. A 20 watt charger needs under one. Real phones slow down near full.
A tablet battery holds twice the energy, so every charger takes twice as long to fill it.

chapters.title: Follow the energy
chapters.lead: From the wall socket to the light of the screen.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: The socket gives 230 volts that swing back and forth. The charger turns it into a low, steady voltage.
In the battery, lithium ions are pushed from one electrode layer to the other. That stores the energy.
Using the phone lets the ions flow back. The current drives the processor, the radio and the screen.
In the end all of it leaves as light, radio waves and heat. That is why a busy phone feels warm.

chapters.title: The number
chapters.lead: A full phone battery holds about 15 watt-hours.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: 4000 milliamp-hours at 3.85 volts is about 15 watt-hours: the energy of one full battery.
Charging it costs under half a cent. A whole year of daily charging is a little over one euro.
A 2 kW kettle uses a phone's full charge in 28 seconds. The phone spends that energy over a whole day.

headline.label: energy in a full phone battery

rows.label: One full charge at 20 cents per kWh

compare.label: A kettle uses the same energy in

objects.label: Metal spoon
objects.detect_hint: a metal spoon, fork, knife or other metal cutlery, in a hand, a cup or on a table
objects.concept: Heat conduction: metal carries heat fast, so a spoon feels cold and gets hot in tea
objects.answer: Metal carries heat away from your skin fast.

chapters.title: How it works
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Up/down: turn it.
captions: Leave a metal spoon in hot tea and the handle soon feels hot.
Heat must travel from the tea, through the bowl, up the handle to your fingers.
Hot tea shakes the metal's atoms; free electrons carry that shaking quickly up the handle.
Wood has no free electrons, so heat creeps along a wooden spoon far more slowly.
100 times: how much faster heat moves through steel than through wood.
That is why pan handles are wood or plastic, and good pans have copper bottoms.

chapters.title: Zoom in
chapters.lead: Metal is a grid of atoms in a sea of loose electrons.
chapters.hint: Pinch: zoom in. Left/right: next lens.
captions: A steel spoon looks smooth and solid. Its secrets are far too small to see.
Three hundred times closer, the steel is a patchwork of tiny crystal grains, each a few hundredths of a millimetre wide.
A hundred thousand times closer still, each grain is a tidy grid of atoms. Loose electrons move between them and help carry heat.

chapters.title: Follow the heat
chapters.lead: Heat runs along the metal from the hot end to your hand.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Hot tea shakes the atoms in the bowl of the spoon. That shaking is heat.
The shaking passes along the metal, helped by loose electrons. In a minute the handle is warm.
Your fingers take the heat from the handle. Some also leaves into the air along the way.

chapters.title: The number
chapters.lead: Steel conducts heat about a hundred times better than wood.
chapters.hint: Pinch: next step. Left/right: next lens.
captions: Steel conducts heat about 100 times better than wood and pulls warmth from your skin much faster. That is why it feels cold.
Both spoons are at room temperature. The steel one only drains the warmth from your skin faster.
Silver conducts 27 times better than steel. A silver spoon in hot tea can get too hot to hold within a minute.

headline.label: how much better stainless steel conducts heat than wood
